title: Place Value Grade 4 Lakhs: Read & Write Big Indian Numbers + Free Quiz
meta_title: Place Value Grade 4 Lakhs: Read & Write Big Numbers
meta_desc: Master place value grade 4 lakhs: read, write and expand big Indian numbers up to lakhs, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable worksheet to practise.
excerpt: In Grade 3 the biggest number was ten thousand. In Grade 4 the road opens up to lakhs — and with it the Indian comma grouping that trips up so many children. Here is how to teach reading, writing and expanding numbers up to a few lakh, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 4 child to write ‘four lakh’ in figures and you will often get 400000 in one unbroken run of zeros, or worse, 40000 — one zero short. This is the exact moment place value grade 4 lakhs starts to matter, because in Grade 3 the ceiling was ten thousand and every number still fit inside four digits. Now the numbers grow a whole period taller, and the Indian way of grouping them with commas is what keeps a six-digit number from turning into a guessing game.

The good news: nothing new is really being invented here. A child who understood ones, tens, hundreds and thousands last year already owns most of the machinery. Grade 4 just bolts two more places on top — ten thousands and lakhs — and teaches a comma rule to read the result out loud.

The Indian place-value system: ones to lakhs

Indian numbers are read in periods. The first period, on the right, is the ones period and holds three places: ones, tens and hundreds. The next period is the thousands period and holds two places: thousands and ten thousands. After that comes the lakhs period. So a number like 4,00,000 has a digit sitting in the lakhs place with five zeros trailing behind it.

Read from the right, the places go: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs. That ordering is worth chanting until it is automatic, because every other skill in this chapter — reading, writing, expanded form — leans on knowing which place a digit sits in.

The place-value chart

I get children to draw this chart once and keep it in the front of their notebook. Any six-digit number can be dropped into it, one digit per column.

PeriodLakhsThousandsOnes
PlaceLakhs (1,00,000)Ten thousands (10,000)Thousands (1,000)Hundreds (100)Tens (10)Ones (1)
3,45,678345678
4,00,000400000
6,07,040607040

The Indian comma rule for lakhs

This is where Indian numbers look different from what a child sees on a calculator screen. The rule is simple once stated plainly:

  • Starting from the right, put the first comma after three digits (that closes the ones period).
  • After that, put a comma after every two digits.

So 500000 becomes 5,00,000 — comma after three, then after two. And 68000 becomes 68,000. The commas are not decoration; they tell you exactly where the lakhs and thousands begin, which is what lets you read the number aloud without counting zeros on your fingers. A child who groups correctly will say ‘five lakh’ on sight instead of squinting at a wall of noughts.

Reading and writing numbers up to a few lakh

Once the commas are in, reading is a matter of naming each period. For 3,45,678 you read the lakhs period first (‘three lakh’), then the thousands period (‘forty-five thousand’), then the ones period (‘six hundred seventy-eight’). Put together: three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred seventy-eight.

Writing works backwards. Give a child ‘two lakh five thousand’ and the trap is the empty places. There is no hundreds, tens or ones, so those columns become zeros: 2,05,000. The single most common Grade 4 error I see is dropping a zero in the middle — writing 2,5,000 or 25,000 instead of 2,05,000. The place-value chart fixes this instantly, because every empty column must still be filled with a 0.

Expanded form and the value of a digit

Every digit carries two different ideas: its face value (the digit itself) and its place value (what it is worth in that column). In 8,14,325 the digit 8 has a face value of 8 but a place value of 8,00,000, because it sits in the lakhs place. The digit 5 has a place value of just 5.

Expanded form makes this visible. You break the number into the sum of each digit’s place value:

  • 4,68,000 = 4,00,000 + 60,000 + 8,000
  • 3,45,678 = 3,00,000 + 40,000 + 5,000 + 600 + 70 + 8

Notice that zeros contribute nothing, so they simply drop out of the expanded form — another reason to make peace with zeros early. A child who can move fluently between the standard number, the words and the expanded form has genuinely understood place value, not just memorised a comma rule.

Indian lakhs vs the international system

Children will meet both systems — the Indian one at home and in NCERT, the international one on phones, spreadsheets and abroad — so it helps to show them side by side rather than pretend one does not exist. The international system groups digits in threes the whole way (thousands, then millions) and calls 1,00,000 a ‘hundred thousand’.

FigureIndian systemInternational system
1,00,000One lakh100,000 – one hundred thousand
3,00,000Three lakh300,000 – three hundred thousand
10,00,000Ten lakh1,000,000 – one million

The comma positions differ, which is exactly why the two look different on paper. My advice: teach the Indian system properly first, then introduce the international grouping as ‘the other way you will sometimes see it’. Trying to teach both at once, in my experience, is how a Grade 4 child ends up trusting neither.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly this material — naming places, the comma rule, expanded form and the Indian-versus-international contrast. Let your child work through it and read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice up to lakhs, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Place Value to Lakhs Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the Indian place-value system up to lakhs — naming places, the comma rule, expanded form and words. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 4 place value of numbers up to lakhs

questions.q: In 3,45,678, which digit is in the ten thousands place?
questions.explanation: Reading from the right the places are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs. The ten thousands place holds the 4.

questions.q: What is the place value of the digit 7 in 7,20,000?
questions.explanation: The 7 sits in the lakhs place, so its place value is 7,00,000 (seven lakh).

questions.q: How is 'two lakh five thousand' written in figures?
questions.explanation: Two lakh is 2,00,000 and five thousand is 5,000, so together it is 2,05,000. The empty hundreds, tens and ones become zeros.

questions.q: Which is the correct expanded form of 4,68,000?
questions.explanation: Break it by place value: 4 lakh + 6 ten-thousands + 8 thousands = 4,00,000 + 60,000 + 8,000.

questions.q: In the Indian system, the first comma from the right is placed after how many digits?
questions.explanation: The first comma goes after three digits to close the ones period, and every comma after that goes after two digits.

questions.q: How do you read 6,07,040 in words?
options: Six lakh seventy thousand four hundred
questions.explanation: The periods read six lakh, seven thousand, and forty in the ones period, giving six lakh seven thousand forty.

questions.q: In the international system, the Indian number 3,00,000 (three lakh) is written as:
questions.explanation: The international system groups in threes and calls it three hundred thousand, written 300,000.

questions.q: Which digit has the greatest place value in 8,14,325?
questions.explanation: The 8 is in the lakhs place, so its place value is 8,00,000 — the largest of all the digits.

faq.q: What place value should a Grade 4 child know?
faq.a: By Grade 4 a child should read, write and expand numbers up to at least a few lakh — that means the ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands and lakhs places, plus the Indian comma grouping. This builds directly on the to-10,000 work from Grade 3.

faq.q: Why are Indian and international commas placed differently?
faq.a: The Indian system closes the ones period after three digits and then groups every two digits, so one lakh is 1,00,000. The international system groups in threes throughout, so the same number is 100,000, read as one hundred thousand. Same value, different grouping.

faq.q: What is the difference between face value and place value?
faq.a: Face value is just the digit itself, while place value is what the digit is worth in its column. In 8,14,325 the 8 has a face value of 8 but a place value of 8,00,000 because it sits in the lakhs place.

faq.q: What is the most common place-value mistake at this level?
faq.a: Dropping a zero in the middle when writing numbers from words — for example writing 2,05,000 as 25,000. A place-value chart fixes this fast, because every empty column must still be filled with a 0.
